desert_p03_001.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_001.text: The Black Gate stood open above a line of waiting carts. Its eastern arch admitted a strip of pale sky; the western side was hidden behind timbers and a mason's hanging screen. Tuo went forward on foot while the drivers waited beside their teams. Yue could hear a chisel, then the sharper sound of somebody ordering it put down. A small boy sat on a stack of bricks with a basket of breakfasts. He was collecting payment more carefully than he counted the bowls. Han bought one for the watchman who had carried yesterday's width notice.

desert_p03_002.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_002.text: The watchman came out with porridge on his chin and said the first grain cart had knocked a stone loose from the eastern jamb. The road was stopped while the mason checked it. Behind them a merchant began demanding to know who would pay for the lost morning. Nobody answered because the mason was already halfway up a ladder. Gao looked at the sky, then at the work, and asked Han to keep the crew beside their carts. She had seen too many delayed travellers use waiting as an opportunity to scatter beyond any useful shouting distance.

desert_p03_003.speaker: han_xun
desert_p03_003.text: We lose the cool hour if we pass the same complaint from cart to cart. We do not recover it by standing under falling stone. Let the mason work. We shall eat here, keep the animals shaded as far as the wall allows, and leave when the opening is safe. If the delay changes our first camp, Tuo will choose another. I would prefer to pay for an hour of waiting than spend the rest of my life explaining why the cook's last meal was porridge taken beneath a badly supported gate.

desert_p03_004.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_004.text: The cook heard and said he would demand a better last meal. Long Legs offered him a sour plum, which he accepted as an improvement. Yue walked the stopping flag back to the third cart, where its driver had started to spread the tank shade toward a patch of rising sunlight. They held the cloth together while the driver fixed its hooks. The mule with the wooden bird's owner tugged once at its lead, then settled. Behind the caravan a pair of orchard carts arrived. Their passengers included a woman carrying a sleeping baby against her shoulder.

desert_p03_005.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_005.text: The merchant's shouting woke the baby. Its mother looked at him with an exhaustion more persuasive than anger. He lowered his voice, though he kept muttering about officials. Yue saw him take a cloth from his own load and make shade across the woman's seat. The mother thanked him. His complaint continued under his breath, now addressed to a crate instead of the entire street. Han noticed too and said nothing. Yue had met people who could be generous only after an argument, and wondered how many friendships began when someone finally put down the need to be right.

desert_p03_006.speaker: tuo_yin
desert_p03_006.text: The upper jamb is sound. The struck stone belongs to the outer facing, but the mason wants to seat its neighbour before traffic resumes. We have perhaps another half hour. I have looked at the nail heads inside the passage; nothing projects into our rack. The paving drops sharply just outside, so the first driver must keep the team straight until the rear wheel clears. I shall stand beyond the drop. Gao, come with me for the line of sight. Yue, stay beside the equipment cart. If you cannot see my flag, do not invent an instruction.

desert_p03_007.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_007.text: The mason descended to fetch a thinner wedge. While he was on the ground, a dog ran through the gate carrying one of the breakfast boy's empty bowls. The boy chased it as far as the nearest brace, then stopped when the watchman caught his collar. A stone clicked against the scaffolding above. Everyone looked up together. It fell into the screen, harmlessly, but the dog disappeared down the street with the bowl. Yue returned the boy's basket to his bricks. He accepted it furiously, then began laughing once the watchman let him hear how ridiculous the dog had looked.

desert_p03_008.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_008.text: Du took the interruption as an invitation to sketch the gate's current outline. Gao returned from the outer road and reminded him that the scaffolding was temporary. He marked it differently, but kept the sketch. The old arch measured fewer paces across than his childhood memory insisted. He had passed through it on a camel cart years earlier, staring up while his father argued about an inspection fee. Gao asked whether the camel had complained too. Du said his father had supplied enough complaint for both. The boy leaned over his drawing and identified the dog as the missing landmark.

desert_p03_009.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_009.text: By the time the mason signalled clearance, the eastern sky was bright. Tuo raised her flag outside the arch; the first driver set the team moving slowly. The folded rack passed beneath the stone cleanly. Yue watched the near wheel cross the paving drop, then looked back at the second cart rather than following it with her feet. The next driver waited for a gap. Their passage made no dramatic noise. On the other side, Han counted three carts and six animals while the last axle settled onto the road. Gao unfolded the rack again before they left the wall.

desert_p03_010.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_010.text: Bitter Wells did not end at its gate. Vegetable plots reached along the road, enclosed by reed screens and ditches. A woman was lifting water with a treadle wheel, her bare feet moving in a soothing rhythm. The wet channels glittered between bean rows. Beyond them lay the pale rise they would climb before the basin appeared. Yue looked back once. Han's daughter stood on a flat roof with a cloth in her hand, too far away for words. Han raised his hat until she lowered the cloth. Then he put it on and watched the road ahead.

desert_p03_011.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_011.text: At first everybody found something to adjust. A blanket slipped; a hat cord tightened across a throat; the cook discovered his ladle making an irritating bell against the stove. Yue's staff cap clicked beside her left sandal until Tuo suggested a different angle. The change eased the sound and the pressure on her shoulder. She tried it for twenty paces before deciding it helped. Her fifth-stage training had made her attentive to the routes through her legs. Walking with a borrowed staff required another kind of listening, down through leather and dust to the places where weight actually landed.

desert_p03_012.speaker: tuo_yin
desert_p03_012.text: You are measuring every step. Good for the first few, tiring for the next thousand. Let the road tell you when something changes. A rising bank, a loose patch, a strap rubbing: those deserve attention. Plain ground deserves enough that you stay upright, then you can look around. I taught my nephew this by making him name birds as he walked. He named every small bird sparrow, which was an efficient method of remaining wrong. Now he guides river carts and sends me letters about water I have never seen. I hope he has improved the birds.

desert_p03_013.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_013.text: At the first rise the carts stopped for a brake check. The grain-cart merchant passed them on a side path intended for foot travellers, his wheels breaking its crust. Long Legs watched with open envy until one wheel sank to its hub. The merchant's workers began unloading bags. Tuo refused to enjoy it loudly. Han sent two drivers to help while the other carts stayed braked on firm ground. Yue carried the red flag farther down the shoulder, where approaching traffic could see a stopped load. The merchant looked ashamed when Han took a bag without mentioning his earlier complaints.

desert_p03_014.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_014.text: The delay cost them fifteen minutes and saved the footpath from a deeper rut. The merchant had chosen it because his buyers expected him by midmorning, and his eldest son had fever at home. Han asked whether the buyers could receive a message. The merchant pointed toward a passing messenger on a bicycle-like treadle cart, who agreed to carry one written line for the usual fee. Du supplied paper. Yue watched the merchant's shoulders lower after the message left. Sometimes a reckless shortcut began with an obligation that had become too large to hold alone.

desert_p03_015.speaker: gao_ru
desert_p03_015.text: Write where the wheel sank, not an opinion about the man. That shoulder looks firm beside the ruts because nobody drives there. Its crust has been drying over softer ground. We have learned something useful before reaching the white plain. Tuo will tell the receiving house on return if the path needs a barrier. For now set two warning flags while the workers refill the shallow hole. Those are the yard's cheap path flags, from the first cart, not our sighting marks. I know the red case is tempting. Its contents would announce a survey beside a bad patch.

desert_p03_016.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_016.text: They carried the little path flags added by Tuo before loading. Yue fetched the bundle and gave its two sticks to a driver with sound hands. She recorded the location from the rise marker, whose chipped number remained readable. Du corrected the spelling of the marker's name and then admitted local people pronounced it three ways. The merchant's cart returned to the public road. Its workers thanked them, one with a nod so slight Yue nearly missed it. The cook climbed onto his seat, said the beans had travelled no farther during all this wisdom, and signalled readiness.

desert_p03_017.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_017.text: Near the lower plain the air began to smell faintly bitter. Dark soil thinned between grass clumps; white fragments appeared in the wheel ruts like spilled flour. Yue bent to look at one while the carts waited for Gao to settle the sighting tripod. Salt lay in a broken skin over damp earth. A beetle crossed it and vanished beneath a green tuft. She had expected the basin to announce itself in a single spectacular view. Instead it approached in small alterations, each ordinary until it joined the next. The staff stood against her shoulder, warmed by the rising sun.

desert_p03_018.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_018.text: Gao used a known roadside marker for the first observation and asked Yue to hold the graduated rod on stone. She chose a place that looked level, then watched the lower edge settle into soil. Gao sent her onto the actual stone. From the instrument's seat, the difference was obvious. From beside the rod it had not been. They repeated the observation after the shaft stopped moving. Du recorded the older marker distance alongside it. Nobody compared figures until both pages were closed. Yue felt foolish about the footing and relieved that the mistake had cost only a few minutes.

desert_p03_019.speaker: gao_ru
desert_p03_019.text: I learned that error on a marsh bank, with a magistrate watching. Every time my assistant breathed, the rod sank a little farther. We discovered a splendidly tilted bridge that did not exist. The magistrate wanted it repaired. I wanted the earth to swallow me after it had finished swallowing the rod. We repeated the work on sound footing, and he was sensible about the correction. That has not stopped him introducing me as the woman who once found a downhill bridge on level water. Accuracy can survive a joke. It does better when we learn to survive one too.

desert_p03_020.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_020.text: Yue held the rod for the second set and let the story loosen her shoulders. A faint wind had risen across the plain. Gao waited through a gust, read, then covered the instrument before the dust thickened. Tuo came back from the bend carrying a dry grass stem. The tracks ahead showed two recent carts, neither likely to be the overdue eastern guides. One wheel print was broad enough to belong to a stone carrier. She explained the limits of the inference when asked. There were many carts of that size; a track did not come with its owner's face.

desert_p03_021.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_021.text: They drank at the first long halt, in shade made by stretching a cart cloth between the loaded frame and two issued shelter poles. The camp worker fixed the poles where the ground held their stakes. Yue's morning portion had warmed despite the covered jar, but tasted better than the cool water she had hurried through in the yard. The drivers checked the mules' mouths before watering, and the farrier walked each animal over a short patch of firm soil. Their labour had its own sequence. Yue stayed out of the way until asked to carry an empty cup.

desert_p03_022.speaker: bao_sun
desert_p03_022.text: Sit for a moment before you decide you feel perfectly well. Your face has been looking at the road, and the road has been looking back rather brightly. Those screens can lower over your eyes without making you a bad reader of things. There. Is the light easier? Good. Eat the fruit now if it helps with appetite. You will not earn an extra meal by saving it until it becomes an object of archaeology. The cook has plenty for the planned days. People who forget to eat become troublesome cargo surprisingly quickly.

desert_p03_023.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_023.text: Yue ate the last sour plum and laughed despite the juice tightening her mouth. Bao sat with her own bowl balanced on one knee. The clinician asked each worker about headache, thirst, and nausea while appearing to discuss lunch. One driver admitted the hat he had chosen was too small. Han produced the spare from the issue chest. Its brim was crooked, and the driver declared it an insult to his face. Bao said his face had suffered greater insults from sunlight and would appreciate the repair. He put it on while the others pretended not to see his relief.

desert_p03_024.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_024.text: The grey mule had found grass beside the halt. Tuo let her crop it while the feed bags were checked, then led her away from a wet hollow where the surface gave under a hoof. Yue watched Plum's muzzle move and wondered whether animals knew more about the ground than their handlers. The farrier offered: sometimes they did, and sometimes the sweetest-looking mouthful stood above a broken drain. He pointed out the old ditch line. Beyond it the grass changed colour. Yue sketched that change in the margin, beside a note to look for support rather than green.

desert_p03_025.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_025.text: After the halt the road turned along a low embankment. Heat blurred the far edge of the basin, making a band of pale sky appear where Yue expected earth. She had read about mirages and still found herself searching for a shore. Du saw her looking and told her the first basin he crossed had seemed full of lakes. He had spent half a day accusing his guide of cruelty for refusing to approach them. Tuo called from ahead that some guides remained cruel for other reasons. Du said she had never needed a mirage to justify hers.

desert_p03_026.speaker: du_she
desert_p03_026.text: My father bought me a little bottle before that journey, to bring him water from the farthest lake. I returned with a bottle of dust and a magnificent explanation. He asked whether dust was cheaper. I told him it was more educational. He kept it on his shelf until he died. I used to think that proved he admired my account. Now I think he liked seeing a plan return in some form, even after the world had refused to fit it. If you bring the shoemaker's girl a stone, bring one the pocket can actually bear.

desert_p03_027.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_027.text: The afternoon wind caught a sheet from Du's open map case before he finished speaking. Yue lifted her flag case away from her body but did not chase the paper under wheels. The third driver halted; Du stepped down; Gao caught the sheet against a thorn bush with her hat. A tear ran through its blank margin. He thanked her and used the field paste from his own repair envelope to back it with thin paper. Tuo watched the care he took. For once she had no comment. Yue suspected the little bottle still belonged somewhere inside that map case.

desert_p03_028.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_028.text: A dust whirl crossed the road later, narrow and quick. Tuo stopped the lead cart well before it arrived; the others halted at their practised gaps. The whirl scattered loose straw and struck the first tank's shade panel, wrenching a hook free. Long Legs waited until the dust passed before climbing down. Yue held the red stopping flag behind the last cart while the driver replaced the hook with one from the repair box. The tank itself was dry beneath its frame. Gao asked her to note wind and damage, then inspect her eyes before declaring the little incident finished.

desert_p03_029.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_029.text: For a moment Yue had wanted to leap toward the flying cloth, as she had leapt toward the cart in Bitter Wells. She told Gao that after they started again. The surveyor said quick movement could be useful, but the caravan had already been standing safely. A lost panel would cost less than a person struck beneath the frame. Yue looked at the mules plodding ahead, indifferent to the conversation. She had earned more precise control of her own force. Learning where action belonged was proceeding by less flattering lessons. Gao did not turn that thought into a speech.

desert_p03_030.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_030.text: Their first planned camp lay farther north than the remaining cool light would comfortably allow. Tuo chose a shorter halt beside a gravel shoulder marked on both current sheets. The place was already used by ordinary carriers and stood above the salt hollow. No water source was promised there. Han accepted the change and marked the day's lost travel time for the following morning's discussion. The people looked disappointed, then grateful as their packs came off. Yue laid the staff beside Gao's case and stretched her fingers. The bandages were dusty but dry; the new skin beneath had not reopened.

desert_p03_031.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_031.text: The worker pitched the shelters on the gravel while the drivers aligned the carts against the expected night wind. Bao selected a treatment corner with enough light left to examine hands and feet. The cook wanted the stove in a sheltered dip; Tuo moved it higher because loose salt crust concealed the dip's wet centre. He grumbled, then found the higher spot cooked more evenly. Yue brought the dry kindling issued with the charcoal and watched the first smoke lean west. Behind them the public road was empty. Bitter Wells had become a line of roofs remembered rather than seen.

desert_p03_032.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_032.text: When the tanks were checked, their day's actual withdrawals totalled one hundred and sixty-eight litres. One thousand seven hundred and twelve remained, including the protected compartment. Han wrote the number once, then shut the water book so the table could hold bowls. The drivers fed the mules while Tuo walked the camp boundary with Gao. Yue sat on her folded cloak and heard the cook announce that tonight's beans were geographically distinct from yesterday's. Long Legs asked whether they had received a permit. The laughter was tired, but it travelled easily across the first small camp of their journey.

desert_p03_033.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_033.text: After supper a bell sounded on the road, too quickly for any of their settled animals. Tuo rose before the others. A rider emerged from the dusk leading a lame mule, one hand against its neck. His coat bore the dust of a longer day than theirs. He called the guide by name and asked whether the farrier would look at a loose shoe. Tuo brought him into the lantern's reach. The man's face was young; his expression looked older. He had been trying to reach Bitter Wells before the gate shut, and had spent the last hour walking.

desert_p03_034.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_034.text: The farrier held the mule's hoof while its rider explained that he carried messages from the quarry. A nail had worked loose and twisted the shoe against soft tissue. The farrier removed it, checked the injured patch, and said the animal should rest instead of walking into town tonight. Han offered the edge of their shelter. The rider looked at the remaining miles, then accepted. He took a cup of water and a bowl from the cook. Han entered the extra litre after the evening total: one thousand seven hundred and eleven now remained. The meal needed no heroic accounting.

desert_p03_035.speaker: tuo_yin
desert_p03_035.text: You came by the upper road? Tell me about the low crossing past the grass shelf. We expected it dry by now. We have three loaded carts, not your narrow feet and an animal that deserves better luck. Yes, sit while you tell me. Nobody here improves a story by suffering through it upright. Start with the time you passed the crossing, then the side you approached. If you rode through water, say how deep against the mule's leg. If somebody told you about it, tell us who. I can use either, provided I know which I am hearing.

desert_p03_036.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_036.text: He had crossed from the north that morning. The ditch carried unexpected water, thin at the western edge and deepening beside the damaged culvert. Quarry drainage had followed an old channel after a bank collapsed. His mule had waded, but a cart would need the stone causeway farther west. Tuo spread the public road sheet and let him point. Du fetched the dated quarry plan from his correspondence. It showed a retaining bank that had existed six weeks ago. Gao marked the new report in pencil, avoiding the firm line she would use after seeing the ground herself.

desert_p03_037.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_037.text: The rider had seen two sign boards beside the culvert. He did not know which routes they had indicated before falling. Tuo asked about the causeway. He had used it last winter and seen its southern approach that morning; the central span was hidden by a rise. The caravan could inspect before committing its wheels. The extra distance would consume part of the margin they had already lost at the gate. Han asked whether returning remained easier than continuing. Tuo said yes, from the next fork. She would not answer for the road beyond a crossing nobody present had inspected.

desert_p03_038.speaker: gao_ru
desert_p03_038.text: We go as far as the fork tomorrow, look, and make the next decision there. This is why our plan names days without treating them as commands. Han, write the delay on the customer's copy when we return. Du, let me take that quarry plan in the morning. Yue, you will sketch the crossing from dry ground if we reach it. You will not measure depth by walking into a drainage channel because the page has room for a figure. Our rider has done enough walking for everybody tonight. The farrier will tell us when his mule should move.

desert_p03_039.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_039.text: The rider's shoulders relaxed as the caravan accepted his news. He had expected anger at the quarry, and perhaps at him for arriving with it. The cook gave him more greens, saying that bad news improved when properly fed. Du asked about the sign boards' lettering; the rider remembered only a blue edge. That was not enough to identify their instructions. Yue wrote the description without filling the gap from the map. The young man began to look his own age again. Tuo lent him a folded blanket and told him to stop apologising to an animal already asleep.

desert_p03_040.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_040.text: Gao and Tuo walked to the low rise beyond camp to compare the approaching road with the visible basin. Yue followed at their invitation, carrying the lantern by its issued loop. The salt plain had lost its brightness and become a dark, shallow space beneath the stars. Far away, several steady lights marked the quarry accommodation. Their apparent distance said little without a reference point. Gao asked Yue to cover the lantern while they looked. In the dark, the road's pale edge became easier to distinguish. It bent toward the crossing, then disappeared behind grass and a low ridge.

desert_p03_041.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_041.text: Tuo described the seasonal watercourses without trying to make them visible. One ran south in a wet summer; another had not flowed openly in years, though its underground seep kept a strip of grass alive. Quarry workers had diverted the first into a settling basin. A failed bank might spill into either. Gao listened, then asked which marks Tuo remembered from her last passage. The guide named two cairns and a dark stone outcrop. One cairn had been reduced by travellers borrowing its stones. They would look for the outcrop, which people could not casually carry home.

desert_p03_042.speaker: tuo_yin
desert_p03_042.text: I dislike remembering a road better than I can see it. At my age people congratulate memory as though it were a second pair of eyes. A remembered cairn is useful until a mason needs five stones. Then it becomes useful chiefly as a warning about pride. My brother used to build little cairns on every walk. He thought roads would be kinder if nobody could miss them. Half the village dismantled his work to mend chicken walls. He would start again without asking for the stones back. I found that both foolish and rather difficult to dislike.

desert_p03_043.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_043.text: Yue heard the first clear mention of Tuo's brother and kept her questions small. Was he also a guide? Tuo said he had driven freight before he learned the basin paths. She did not say what had happened to him. Gao turned toward camp, giving the conversation a natural end. They carried the covered lantern between them until the stove glow showed below the rise. Yue had wanted to ask more and felt the desire settle when she saw Tuo's face. A person could offer one piece of a story without having agreed to empty the whole box.

desert_p03_044.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_044.text: Du sat beside the stove trying to dry his repaired map sheet without curling it. The cook had warned him twice about the flame. Gao laid a board across two stones and helped him weight the corners. He thanked her, then asked whether she still drew a tiny bird beside difficult observations. She looked annoyed, which answered him. Yue glanced at the field book and found a wing beneath today's unstable staff reading. Gao said it marked an observation to revisit, not a failure. Du admitted his first book had been full of birdlike marks, though his attempts resembled forks.

desert_p03_045.speaker: gao_ru
desert_p03_045.text: He taught me to keep the hard readings where I could see them. Then, when I passed the licensing trial, he offered me work copying fair sheets instead of making observations. He thought I would prefer a secure desk. I thought he believed I had passed by luck. We did not ask each other the obvious question for nearly a year. I took field work with another surveyor and sent him a very sharp letter. He sent back three corrections to my distances and no answer to my accusation. You may imagine how soothing that was to receive.

desert_p03_046.speaker: du_she
desert_p03_046.text: I remember the letter. I kept it because nobody before you had told me I could be patronising in seven distinct ways within one paragraph. I thought the desk paid better and spared you the worst roads. You thought I had put a leash on your ambitions. By the time I understood, you were measuring a mountain road better than my office could. I should have asked. I have practised asking since, with uneven success. If you wish to show Yue the letter, I request that you at least explain the circumstances before reading the second insult aloud.

desert_p03_047.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_047.text: Gao laughed and said the second insult was the one she regretted. The cook demanded to hear it, on the grounds that regretted insults were often the best. Du refused with dignity for a man holding a map over a bean stove. Yue watched the old disagreement become shared comedy without disappearing. Their work together did not mean everything had been forgiven in a single good conversation. It meant they had returned often enough to know where laughter could rest. Tuo came back with the lantern and asked whether the north road had moved while everyone admired their own youth.

desert_p03_048.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_048.text: Bao called Yue to the treatment corner. Her palms were healing beneath dusty wraps, but the right sandal had raised a small blister below the changed strap. Bao drained nothing; she protected the spot and explained where to adjust the fastening in the morning. Yue was embarrassed to have noticed it only after sitting down. Bao said feet often waited until a person stopped giving them orders. She checked the drivers too. Long Legs had a rubbed heel and blamed his bucket, which had remained in the yard. The clinician admired the distance over which he could extend a grievance.

desert_p03_049.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_049.text: The rider's mule settled with the animals, separated enough that its loosened shoe would not be struck. The farrier had fitted a temporary protective wrap from his own supplies. He could replace the shoe after checking the tender patch at dawn. The rider sent his quarry letters ahead with an evening carrier bound for Bitter Wells, retaining the payment receipt. He no longer had to choose between timely news and an injured animal. Han offered to witness the handover, then stood aside while the two men counted the sealed packets themselves. Trust did not require pretending packets had no destinations.

desert_p03_050.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_050.text: Yue walked back to her shelter through a lane between carts. The night sky had become crowded in a way she had forgotten inside towns. Plum lifted her head when Yue passed, sniffed the bandages, and decided there was nothing to eat. The girl sat outside her tent briefly, staff laid beside her, and tried to identify the dark shapes on the horizon. She could name none with confidence. The basin looked less like the map than the yard had. That difference had frightened her earlier; now it seemed like the beginning of learning what the map was for.

desert_p03_051.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_051.text: Han came by with a lamp and asked whether the shelter was comfortable. Yue said it was, apart from a stone under her hip. He knelt, reached beneath the groundcloth, and removed it. For a man responsible for contracts, he seemed oddly relieved by a problem he could hold in his hand. He told her the deposit keeper had sent confirmation that every return claim was filed. The message had arrived just after they left town and caught them here. Then he stood too quickly, struck his head on the tent pole, and swore softly.

desert_p03_052.speaker: han_xun
desert_p03_052.text: The daughter will hear of that before I get home. Long Legs has eyes like a hawk for anything that happens to somebody else. He cannot find the place where he put his bowl. I should not say that about a man driving my water, but he already knows. You have done enough. Tomorrow may demand a different road. Sleep now; the figures will remain troublesome without your help. If the wind grows loud, the camp worker will check the lines. You do not need to come out every time a tent decides to complain.

desert_p03_053.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_053.text: A tent did complain after midnight. The sound woke Yue halfway into a dream of floating bowls. She heard footsteps, a low exchange, then the firmer snap of a tightened line. The expected night wind had arrived from the west. Her own shelter shifted, but held. She resisted sitting up, listened long enough to recognise the camp worker's voice, and lay back. In the kiln she had learned to recover between demanding trials. On the road recovery depended partly on letting other people perform the work for which they were awake. The thought became sleep before she finished considering it.

desert_p03_054.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_054.text: At dawn the rider's mule placed its foot more comfortably. The farrier fitted a sound shoe, warned against a hard pace, and accepted the rider's payment for the new nails rather than the help itself. The young man would walk to town beside the animal. He thanked the caravan, taking a piece of breakfast bread for the road. Bao checked his water bottle before he left; he had filled it from his own remaining travel jar. Tuo sent a short crossing report with him to the receiving house, dated and clearly labelled as information received rather than an inspection.

desert_p03_055.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_055.text: The camp came apart with less confusion than yesterday's loading rehearsal. Yue found the staff without looking beneath three blankets. The drivers emptied their bedding places before releasing the cart brakes. The cook shook ash from the stove into the agreed waste pit, dampened it with a small recorded portion of his cooking allowance, and covered it with gravel. Bao checked that nobody had packed a wet dressing beside food. Tuo collected the cheap path flags at the camp entrance; this shoulder needed no new warning left behind. By the time the first cart moved, the tents were sacks again.

desert_p03_056.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_056.text: At the morning fork Gao asked Yue to sketch the two approaches before reading the plan. One road curved toward the reported drainage crossing. The other climbed a shallow bank westward, its ruts interrupted by dry grass. Tuo walked both entrances while the animals rested. Fresh cart tracks used the western approach, but their condition showed only that carts had gone there, not that they had reached the far side. Yue drew the changed grass line and the fallen sign board. It had fallen face down. They would need to examine it before giving its blue edge a meaning.

desert_p03_057.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_057.text: Han looked at the eastern road with obvious reluctance. It was shorter and smoother, exactly the sort of road his customer expected him to prefer. The water book and yesterday's delay gave him reasons to hurry. He opened neither while Tuo went to inspect. Gao stayed beside him, studying the western rise. When he asked what she thought, she said the choice would become easier after ten minutes of seeing. He shut his mouth around an unfinished objection. Yue recognised the cost of that silence. Han's business depended on turning uncertain journeys into dates other people could use.

desert_p03_058.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_058.text: Tuo returned with mud on one sandal and water darkening the tip of her staff. From firm ground she had seen the eastern culvert partly blocked by quarry debris. The shallow edge could tempt a mule, but the loaded carts would enter a softer channel. She recommended the western causeway if its central span passed inspection. That meant an extra climb and a visit to the grass shelf people whose grazing ground bordered it. Han agreed. The cook began complaining about beans having to travel uphill. Long Legs asked whether they had ever tried marching downhill of their own accord.

desert_p03_059.speaker: gao_ru
desert_p03_059.text: We shall keep the wheel road, stop before the causeway, and inspect the span on foot. Yue, your sketch of the crossing is enough; do not go after a dramatic angle down that bank. Put the blue board beside the culvert in the report as fallen. We may lift it from dry ground if the camp worker can reach it safely, but it will not decide where we drive. A sign tells us what somebody meant a route to be. Today the water tells us what it has become. The two can disagree without either having a secret motive.

desert_p03_060.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_060.text: The board could not be reached without leaning over the soft bank, so they left it. Du marked its position beside the quarry notation. He did not enjoy leaving an unread sign, but showed no inclination to turn his curiosity into somebody else's heavy task. The first cart took the rise. Yue followed with staff and flags, seeing the eastern road fall away beneath them. The new route led through a strip of green that looked startling after the lower plain. A flock of small birds rose from the grass, too quickly for her to decide whether they were sparrows.

desert_p03_061.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_061.text: From the ridge the causeway appeared as a low line of dark stone above a white hollow. Two people stood near its southern entrance. One wore a broad felt hat; the other carried a bundle of cut grass across his back. Neither waved. Tuo raised an open hand and stopped the lead cart well short of them. Yue set the red flag for the others. The felt-hatted figure looked at the three loads, then at the salt hollow. A goat bleated somewhere out of sight. Gao stepped down beside Tuo, carrying no instrument until they knew where sound footing began.

desert_p03_062.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_062.text: The nearer person was an old woman, taller than Yue expected when she came forward. She asked whether the caravan had seen the broken culvert. Tuo answered plainly. The woman spat into the grass and said the quarry had promised that bank would hold through the wet season. Her companion set down his load. They were moving fodder across the causeway before the hollow deepened. The road remained open, but one stone had shifted near the middle. They would show it if the carts waited. Han thanked them instead of asking first how long the inspection might take.

desert_p03_063.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_063.text: Yue looked beyond the causeway toward the day's road. Yesterday it had been a line between named places. This morning its continuation depended on an old woman's knowledge, a loose shoe, quarry water, and people willing to wait while a stone was examined. She took out the field book and wrote the causeway's approach beside her sketch. There was room for another line beneath it. The woman had begun walking, her hat tilting back in the wind. Tuo followed. Gao motioned Yue to stay beside the carts until called. She obeyed, then began watching where the goats placed their feet.

desert_p03_064.speaker: narrator
desert_p03_064.text: One goat crossed the causeway's outer edge, paused at a clump of grass, and stepped around a darker patch. Its lightness could not certify a cart road, yet the movement made Yue look harder. Water stood against the stone's northern face, hidden from this approach. The surface carried thin streaks of pale sediment. She called Gao back before the surveyor crossed farther. Gao came, crouched beside the first stone, and followed her gaze. Tuo and the old woman waited at the middle. The delayed journey had found its next question in a place yesterday's map showed as a narrow line.

desert_dilemma_causeway_1.speaker: narrator
desert_dilemma_causeway_1.text: Yue wrote that the carts were held pending a support inspection and gave no predicted reopening hour. The messenger left while the booking round was still open. Han retained a receiving slot only on the condition that he updated it after the inspection; another carrier took the earlier place. Yue watched the messenger disappear behind the rise. Her notice had protected the waiting crew from an invented timetable. It had also surrendered an advantage that a confident promise might have kept for one more hour.

desert_dilemma_causeway_2.speaker: narrator
desert_dilemma_causeway_2.text: Yue left the notice unfinished until Tuo called back the shifted stone's position. She could now distinguish an observed movement from an unexamined support beneath it. By the time the messenger departed, the booking round would already be closing. Han accepted that their receiving place might need renegotiation. The sharper account would help a later repair crew, but the waiting drivers would bear today's uncertainty. Yue entered the dispatch time beside the observation, keeping the useful detail and its delay on the same page.

desert_dilemma_causeway_3.speaker: narrator
desert_dilemma_causeway_3.text: Gao approved the short stable shoulder, and Yue walked it without approaching the loose stone. The second view showed where water stood against the causeway's face; it did not expose the buried support. She returned with an exterior sketch while Han dictated a provisional holding message. Preparing both cost their spare quiet interval before departure. Gao kept the sketch separate from the inspection verdict. Yue could offer another angle because she had trained for the ordinary walk, not because a fifth-stage cord let her stand on doubtful ground.

desert_dilemma_causeway.speaker: narrator
desert_dilemma_causeway.text: From beside the braked carts, Yue could see the causeway's surface and none of its buried support. Han needed a delay notice before the receiving yard's next booking round. Tuo and the old woman were already examining the middle stones. Yue could write a cautious holding notice now, wait for their specific observation, or gather a second exterior view from the checked shoulder. No option authorised a wheel to cross. They differed in who waited, what the notice could say, and whether a messenger carried it in time.

choices.text: Send the holding notice now, with support unverified.
Wait for Tuo's observed stone before describing the fault.
Take the checked shoulder view before drafting.
